options: The total length of the path an object actually travels
The straight line from start to finish
How far north an object ends up
The time an object spends moving
questions.explanation: Distance is the total path length — all the meters actually covered, even when the route bends.
questions.misconception: A familiar mix-up is treating distance as the straight line 'as the crow flies' — but that defines displacement, and distance counts the full winding path instead.

questions.prompt: A hiker walks 8 m forward, then no back. What is the total distance traveled?
questions.explanation: Distance adds the two legs together: 8 m out plus 8 m back = 16 m. Distance never subtracts — it only grows as you cover ground.
questions.misconception: Some try to 'cancel' the return leg because you end where you started. That subtraction belongs to displacement, not distance.

questions.prompt: In the model, the winding path reads 25 m and the straight shortcut reads 9 m. Which statement is correct?
options: Both distances are the same because they end between the same gates
questions.explanation: Distance is the full path length (25 m); displacement is the straight line from start to finish (9 m).
questions.misconception: The instinct to average both readings or make them equal is common; the two quantities are independent — the challenge is they're measured the same maps but answer different questions.

questions.prompt: Which unit is the standard measuring stick for distance?
questions.explanation: The meter (m) is the SI unit of distance. Seconds measure time, kilograms measure mass, and volts measure voltage.
questions.misconception: Learners sometimes recycle time or mass units because they've used them in other problems; the model's readout keeps length in meters even though a stopwatch is also visible.

questions.prompt: A runner covers 200 m in 40 s. Which calculation uses distance correctly to find speed?
questions.explanation: Speed = distance ÷ time, so 200 m ÷ 40 s = 5 m/s — distance is the meter count fed into the ratio.
questions.misconception: Some invert the fraction (s ÷ m). Unit-checking: dividing meters by seconds does give m/s, and meters × seconds gives m·s, a meaningless unit.
